## SBIN — State Bank of India

**PROBABLE** (a subsidiary's listing is in motion (DRHP / board approval)) · **PRE-SPIN — study the parent; the pieces do not trade yet** · score 6.2/10 · partial spin-off / listing · 12 filing(s) from CALLS, NSE · first 2026-03-19, latest 2026-07-17

> **Listing:** IPO / listing of the subsidiary in motion since 2026-03-19; date not fixed — No listing date stated. Filings said (July 11, 2026) "Allotment is expected to take place on or about July 18, 2026"; IPO open July 14, 2026, closing July 16, 2026. Chairman, May 8, 2026: "hopefully in this financial year we will be able to complete"

**Stated in the filings:** size hint: 0.7% of income.

**What is being separated, as the documents put it:** SBI Funds Management Limited, the bank's asset management (mutual fund) subsidiary, partially listed via offer for sale — class `value_unlocking`.

- *Insiders:* SBI sells only up to 4.8851% (cut from 6.3007%) and retains the rest — "we are not fully exiting... still have potential to monetize further"; employees got Rs.54/share discount and ESOPs
- *What it reveals:* A dominant AMC carried at cost: total income Rs.4,969.09 crores, only 0.70% of SBI Group income, reserves Rs.3,533.09 crores; priced at Rs.574/share. Chairman cites "hidden reserves... in terms of strategic investments" not marked to market, plus Rs.2,200 crores special dividend
- *Selling pressure:* unlikely — Book-built IPO to bidding investors and 30 pre-IPO buyers, not distributed to SBI holders; no index exclusion stated
- *Parent or spin:* parent · *option pricing date:* Price band fixed July 8, 2026 at Rs.545 to Rs.574; Offer Price decided at Rs.574.00 per Equity Share on July 16, 2026
- *Read next:* SBIFM Prospectus dated July 16, 2026 — AUM, PAT and implied valuation at Rs.574 versus SBI's retained stake
- *In their words:* “State Bank of India has been informed that the Offer Price for the Offer has been decided to be Rs. 574.00 per Equity Share.”

### Why the demerger — three years of calls and the scheme

The business being separated is SBI Funds Management Limited (SBIFM) — SBI Mutual Fund, the bank's asset-management joint venture with Amundi — which SBI is partially separating by listing it, not by demerging it; management repeatedly framed the purpose as "value unlocking" and, in Chairman C.S. Setty's words, "more importantly, value recognition for the industry" (Nov 2025), with SBI General Insurance named alongside AMC as the other listing candidate. The driver management gave was that SBI's own stock does not reflect the conglomerate's worth: Setty called SBI's valuation "a conundrum, considering our return on equity and growth metrics" (Nov 2025, with ROE 19.7%–20.68% and ROA >1% through FY26), and the same theme runs through the hidden-value argument on strategic holdings — of the group's ~7.3% NSE stake he said "the moment NSE gets listed, the whole shareholding by SBI will be available as reserve to us to mark to market" (May 2026). Explicitly NOT a capital-need story at first: in Nov 2025 Setty said "these two companies do not require capital at this juncture. Neither the parent requires because we just raised Rs. 25,000 crores" (the July 2025 QIP, India's largest, 4.5x oversubscribed on a >Rs. 1.1 trillion book, >60% cross-border), which is why timing was left to "respective boards"; by May 2026 the rationale had hardened into a capital one — the listing "will result in capital augmentation, CET-1" on top of CAR already up 115bps to 15.4%. The structure confirms it is monetisation, not a fix for the business: the IPO is a pure offer for sale (no fresh issue), SBI offering 6.3007% and JV partner Amundi India Holding 3.7006%, total up to 10.0013% / 203,709,239 shares at Rs. 1 face value, so no money reaches SBIFM itself. Management stressed that separation does not break the franchise link — SBIFM stays the country's largest AMC inside the "One SBI" cross-sell engine (a special dividend of ~Rs. 2,200 crore came up to the bank in Q3FY26, cross-sell/CVE income targeted at $1 billion, YONO "deep integration with subsidiary production"), and Setty was explicit that "Mutual fund, we are not fully exiting. So we still have potential to monetize further when market improves" (Feb 2026). The push came from the sell side and retail investors — Sushil Choksey (Indus Equity), Manoj Alimchandani and Kunal Shah (Citigroup) raised monetisation/value-unlocking on four of the five calls, Alimchandani even arguing in Feb 2026 that delaying the IPO five years could fetch three times the market cap — rather than from lenders or regulators; the only regulator-linked nudge cited was the SEBI chairman on NSE's listing. No problem with SBIFM's performance was ever offered as a reason: it was described only as "the largest AMC in the country," contributing Rs. 4,969.09 crore of FY26 total income, just 0.70% of group income.

**How it evolved:** May 2025 had no separation plan at all — only "we will continue to nurture these subsidiaries," while the bank instead took an enabling resolution for Rs. 25,000 crore of its own equity. By Aug 2025 Setty conceded "a couple of candidates for listing, but… there is no sense of urgency," and in Nov 2025 he named them — SBI AMC and SBI General — as the right candidates for "value unlocking" and "value recognition," with boards to set timing; the SBIFM stake-sale approval for 6.3007% followed on 6 Nov 2025 and the DRHP on 19 Mar 2026 (share count restated to 128,334,397 after a bonus issue and ESOP exercises). Feb 2026 added the retained-upside caveat ("we are not fully exiting") and May 2026 re-cast the deal as CET-1 capital augmentation to be completed within FY27. The plan then changed in execution in July 2026: a pre-IPO placement of 28,832,748 shares (1.4156%) to 30 investors at Rs. 574 for Rs. 1,655 crore on 9–10 July cut SBI's offer-for-sale from 6.3007% to 4.8851% (total offer 8.3933%), priced at Rs. 574 with allotment expected 18 July 2026.

**What management expects from it:** For SBIFM: a listed market price that recognises India's largest AMC, with SBI retaining control, banca distribution and future monetisation upside. For SBI: value unlocking and "value recognition," CET-1 capital augmentation supporting 13-15% credit growth, hidden reserves surfaced (as with NSE), and valuation converging on >1% ROA and 15%+ through-cycle ROE. No margin or focus benefit was claimed.

**Point by point, with the source:**

- *[May 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=bba71336-f98b-40e2-8d50-c9435948876b.pdf)* — No separation on the table: subsidiaries framed purely as value creators to be retained, while the bank instead took an enabling resolution to raise Rs. 25,000 crore of its own equity. “Our subsidiaries are consistently performing well and continue to create significant value for all the stakeholders. We will continue to nurture these subsidiaries and maintain leadership position in the respective businesses.”
- *[Aug 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=2fa1b8da-c066-4091-b913-b10127270df1.pdf)* — First acknowledgement of listing candidates, asked for by Sushil Choksey (Indus Equity Advisors); Setty explicitly de-prioritised it because the Rs. 25,000 crore QIP had just closed. “No, as we mentioned that we definitely have a couple of candidates for listing, but the timing is not very… there is no sense of urgency there, I believe.”
- *[Nov 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=ad15487a-d1a9-4e33-90e9-624255749750.pdf)* — The rationale stated in full for the first time, in answer to Choksey on the group's underperforming consolidated value: SBI AMC and SBI General named, with value unlocking and industry recognition of value as the purpose. “But among these four major subsidiaries, we definitely would be looking at, as I mentioned several times, SBI AMC and SBI General are right candidates for listing in our stable. It also provides some value unlocking and, more importantly, value recognition for the industry.”
- *[Nov 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=ad15487a-d1a9-4e33-90e9-624255749750.pdf)* — Answering Kunal Shah (Citigroup) on what would trigger the decision, Setty ruled capital need out as a motive for either the subsidiaries or the parent, leaving timing and quantum to the subsidiary boards. “I think we need to just look at, see, one is, as I mentioned earlier also, that these two companies do not require capital at this juncture.”
- *[Nov 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=ad15487a-d1a9-4e33-90e9-624255749750.pdf)* — The underlying grievance the separation is meant to address — SBI's own market valuation not tracking its ROE and growth — stated in the Chairman's opening remarks; Ashok Ajmera had quantified it as a Rs. 8.82 lakh crore market cap on Rs. 100 trillion of business versus Rs. 15.14 lakh crore for a Rs. 57 trillion peer. “Although the current valuations of SBI are a conundrum, considering our return on equity and growth metrics, we are confident that they will eventually align with our fundamental and operational metrics, the institutionalized nature of our business and our market leadership in the coming years.”
- *[Feb 2026](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=8fabbe0f-593e-4701-b565-d5fce57385a2.pdf)* — Retained-stake logic: asked by Manoj Alimchandani whether delaying the IPO five years could treble the market cap, Setty defended a partial sale that keeps future upside with SBI. “Mutual fund, we are not fully exiting. So we still have potential to monetize further when market improves.”
- *[Feb 2026](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=8fabbe0f-593e-4701-b565-d5fce57385a2.pdf)* — Why the AMC is worth separating while staying attached: it is already the country's largest AMC, upstreamed a Rs. 2,200 crore special dividend into SBI's Q3FY26 profit, and feeds a cross-sell income stream management targets at $1 billion. “If I have to talk about one-off, I think the one item which is a special dividend we have received, around Rs. 2,200 crores from SBI Mutual Fund.”
- *[May 2026](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=9a3280a0-5ce9-445e-a881-6b7c505e9a90.pdf)* — The rationale shifts to capital: with the AMC listing under way, Setty tied it to CET-1 augmentation supporting credit growth (the bank could already fund ~Rs. 12 trillion of growth, CAR 15.4%, up 115bps YoY). “We are also seriously, as you are aware, we have embarked on listing SBI AMC and hopefully in this financial year we will be able to complete, which will result in capital augmentation, CET-1.”
- *[May 2026](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=9a3280a0-5ce9-445e-a881-6b7c505e9a90.pdf)* — Same hidden-value argument applied to the group's ~7.3% NSE holding, which is not marked to market today — listing is the mechanism that converts unrecognised strategic stakes into reported reserves. “But as you mentioned, I think the moment NSE gets listed, the whole shareholding by SBI will be available as reserve to us to mark to market.”
- *Scheme* — 6 Nov 2025 board approval, restated in the 19 Mar 2026 DRHP filing: a pure offer for sale of up to 10.0013% (203,709,239 shares of Rs. 1 each) — SBI 6.3007% (128,334,397 shares) and JV partner Amundi India Holding 3.7006% (75,374,842 shares). No fresh issue, so no proceeds go to SBIFM. “The IPO comprises an offer for sale of up to 128,334,397 Equity Shares (amounting to 6.3007% of the paid-up equity share capital of SBIFML) by State Bank of India, and of up to 75,374,842 Equity Shares (amounting to 3.7006% of the paid-up equity share capital of SBIFML) by Amundi India Holding.”
- *Scheme* — Plan changed in execution: a pre-IPO secondary placement on 9–10 July 2026 moved 1.4156% of pre-offer capital to 30 investors at the eventual Rs. 574 offer price, raising Rs. 1,655 crore for SBI ahead of the book build. “State Bank of India had entered into share purchase agreements each dated July 9, 2026 to sell, in aggregate, 2,88,32,748 equity shares of SBIFM of face value Rs. 1 (one) each ("Equity Shares"), being equivalent to 1.4156% of pre-Offer share capital of SBIFM, to a total of 30 (thirty) investors at Rs. 574.00 per Equity Share, for an aggregate consideration of Rs. 1,655.00 crores.”
- *Scheme* — The 11 July 2026 addendum cut SBI's offer-for-sale by exactly the pre-IPO quantum, to 4.8851% (total offer 8.3933%); the offer was priced at Rs. 574 on 16 July with a Rs. 54 employee discount and allotment expected on or about 18 July 2026. “The size of the offer for sale by the State Bank of India in the IPO has been revised from up to 128,334,397 Equity Shares (amounting to 6.3007% of the paid-up equity share capital of SBIFM) to up to 99,501,649 Equity Shares (amounting to 4.8851% of the paid-up equity share capital of SBIFM).”

*Not explained on the calls:* No valuation target, expected proceeds, CET-1 basis points, or use of funds; no reason the offer was trimmed; Amundi's motive, SBI General's timeline, and post-listing distribution/royalty terms unexplained.

## ASHOKLEY — Ashok Leyland Ltd.

**PROBABLE** (a scheme of arrangement whose nature the documents on file do not settle) · **PRE-SPIN — study the parent; the pieces do not trade yet** · score 5.8/10 · scheme (nature unclear) · 3 filing(s) from NSE · first 2026-05-20, latest 2026-11-05

> **Listing:** NOT YET — scheme at 'nclt_sanction' stage; the resulting company will list only after NCLT sanction, effectiveness and a record date; indicated timeline: Nov 12, 2025 call: "HLF has received the final clearance from RBI to initiate a merger process with NXT Digital, paving the way for its listing. The listing process is progressing as per plan"; same call: listing "could take a minimum of the Q1 of the next financial year"; Feb 11, 2026 call: "with all the necessary approvals in place, the process is being followed for a final closure"; May 28, 2026 call: "should get consummated within this or the next quarter"; NCLT sanctioned Nov 3, 2026 and the Scheme "shall become effective upon filing of the certified copy of the NCLT order with the Registrar of Companies"

**The stages, as filed:** nclt_sanction (2026-11-05)

**Stated in the filings:** entitlement **25 for every 10**.

**What is being separated, as the documents put it:** Hinduja Leyland Finance's non-banking finance (vehicle and housing finance) business, absorbed into listed shell NDL Ventures Limited — class `value_unlocking`.

- *Insiders:* Ashok Leyland's stake dilutes from 61.12% in HLFL to 59.64% in NDL, which becomes its material listed subsidiary; "No specific benefit is proposed to accrue to the promoter, promoter group or group companies."
- *What it reveals:* A large NBFC enters a near-empty listed shell: NDL turnover only ₹489.37 lakhs (FY26) versus HLF AUM ~₹59,000 crores and PAT ₹491 crores, HHF ~₹16,000 crores AUM. Official Liquidator flagged overdue loans, near-term repayments and FVTOCI loan valuations.
- *Selling pressure:* likely — HLFL's previously unlisted holders receive listed NDL shares, 25 for every 10; index or size effects not stated.
- *Parent or spin:* spin · *option pricing date:* not stated
- *Read next:* NDL's record date and post-scheme shareholding pattern, plus HLFL's ECL provisions and FVTOCI loan fair valuation flagged by the Official Liquidator.
- *In their words:* “Upon the Scheme becoming effective, HLFL shall stand dissolved without winding up and shall cease to be a material subsidiary of the Company and consequently NDL shall become the material listed subsidiary of the Company.”

### Why the demerger — three years of calls and the scheme

The business being separated is Ashok Leyland's vehicle- and housing-finance arm — Hinduja Leyland Finance Ltd (HLFL), together with its subsidiary Hinduja Housing Finance (HHF) — which is being taken out of the Ashok Leyland consolidated structure and given its own listing via a reverse merger (merger by absorption) of HLFL into the already-listed NDL Ventures Ltd (formerly NXTDIGITAL), a near-empty vehicle with FY26 turnover of only ₹489.37 lakhs whose objects were amended to permit NBFC business. Management's first stated reason is valuation: Shenu Agarwal said on the May 2025 call that 'our share price of Ashok Leyland actually does not fully reflect the value that we have in our subsidiaries', and Dheeraj Hinduja closed the same call saying HLF and HHF 'do not really figure as we see it showing a true value in Ashok Leyland shares today, but it will through the listing process unlock this' — 'value unlocking from subsidiaries' was one of the six stated medium-term goals alongside mid-teen EBITDA and 35% MHCV share. The second reason is capital: the finance books were compounding 15–26% a year (HLFL standalone AUM ₹42,000cr on+off book in Nov 2023, ₹44,400cr Dec-24, ₹48,000cr Mar-25, ₹50,430cr Jun-25, ₹52,635cr Sep-25, ₹56,470cr Dec-25, ~₹59,000cr Mar-26; HHF ₹13,400cr to ~₹16,000cr), and Balaji repeatedly said growth was being throttled by capital — 'their business opportunities are restricted with the availability of the cash... the Tier-1 capital is also pretty low where RBI has been insisting on the requirement of more investment in Hinduja Leyland Finance' (Nov 2025), and again in Feb 2026 and Jun 2026 that 'Tier 1 capital sometimes is low compared to the peers.' Ashok Leyland had been plugging that gap itself — ₹200cr into HLFL in Q4 FY25 to meet RBI capital adequacy, with carrying value rising from ~₹60 to ~₹64 per AL share — so a listed platform lets HLFL raise its own growth equity instead: the Scheme rationale says HLFL 'will need growth capital to accelerate growth' and that listing 'will increase the avenues for raising growth capital both from public and interested investors', giving 'greater efficiency in capital raising by the merged entity, and unfettered access to both cash flow generated by the business and external capital raising.' The Scheme adds housekeeping benefits: avoidance of duplicated administrative functions, 'reduction in multiplicity of legal and regulatory compliances and cost', an increase in the transferee's net worth, and 'higher level of corporate governance as required by listed entity.' It is being done as a reverse merger rather than an IPO (swap of 25 NDL shares of ₹10 for every 10 HLFL shares of ₹10), which dilutes Ashok Leyland from 61.12% in HLFL to 59.64% in NDL, with NDL becoming the material listed subsidiary and HLFL dissolved without winding up; metrics cited alongside were PAT ₹160cr/qtr (Q1 FY26) rising to ₹220cr (Q3 FY26), FY26 HLF PAT ₹491cr (+20%) and HHF PAT ₹387cr (+4%), CAR 18.2%, GNPA 3.5%/NNPA 2.1% (FY25) improving to consolidated NNPA ~1.4%.

**How it evolved:** The listing was already in train by the Nov 2023 call, when Gopal Mahadevan said HLFL expected it 'sometime in Q4' and flagged that 'it's a reverse merger, there are a lot of compliance that are to be done additionally other than a standard DRHP'; by Feb 2025 it was 'on track... likely to be concluded by the end of Q1 FY26.' In May 2025 the rationale was reframed explicitly as value unlocking after repeated analyst prodding (Raghunandhan, Pramod Kumar), with management conceding delay pending approvals; Aug 2025 brought RBI's final clearance to merge with NXT Digital and Balaji's long list of remaining steps (valuers, swap ratio, RBI/exchange intimation, ROC, SEBI, EGM, NCLT) with a 'minimum of 2, 3 quarters' guide, while simultaneously disclosing RBI pressure on Tier-1 capital. Nov 2025 said it was 'progressing as per plan', the boards of HLFL and NDL approved the Scheme on 25 November 2025 (appointed date 1 April 2026) — prompting a 27 November 2025 rumour-verification filing correcting a report that Ashok Leyland's own board had approved it — then Feb 2026 admitted 'some initial delays' with approvals now in place, and the Jun 2026 call (Q4 FY26) said it 'should get consummated within this or the next quarter'; shareholders and unsecured creditors approved on 30 July 2026 (100% of HLFL equity by value, 99.99% of unsecured creditors) and NCLT Mumbai sanctioned it on 3 November 2026.

**What management expects from it:** For Ashok Leyland: the holding-company discount closed, HLF/HHF value visible in the share price, and an end to recurring equity injections (₹200cr in Q4 FY25) made for RBI capital adequacy, while retaining 59.64% of a listed NBFC. For the finance arm: direct public and investor access to growth capital and Tier-1, higher net worth, fewer duplicated compliances, focused management and listed-company governance to sustain 15–25% AUM growth.

**Point by point, with the source:**

- *[Nov 2023](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=81d9af88-f09b-46cf-9d71-911fe2dbbb91.pdf)* — Mahadevan frames the HLFL listing as a reverse merger expected in Q4 FY24, warning it carries extra compliance versus a normal IPO; total HLFL book then ~₹42,000cr on- and off-book, with HHF called one of the fastest-growing housing finance companies. “I think they are expecting this to happen sometime in Q4. Some it's a reverse merger, there are a lot of compliance that are to be done additionally other than a standard DRHP.”
- *[Feb 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=0d3aa1f2-ea99-41c2-87ea-45bfc80036d8.pdf)* — Reverse merger of HLFL into NDL Ventures declared on track for conclusion by end of Q1 FY26, alongside AUM growth of 26% (HLF ₹44,400cr) and 43% (HHF ₹13,400cr); the board simultaneously approved ₹200cr more equity into HLFL to support its capital adequacy. “The reverse merger of Hinduja Leyland Finance with NDL Ventures is on track. As mentioned earlier, this is likely to be concluded by the end of Q1 FY26.”
- *[May 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=d25ed8e8-c096-4919-b14b-1b1a488ac72f.pdf)* — Agarwal states the separation's purpose is closing a holding-company discount — AL's share price does not reflect subsidiary value — and Dheeraj Hinduja lists 'value unlocking from subsidiaries' among the six medium-term goals; HLFL consolidated AUM ~₹62,000cr (+25%), revenue ₹6,281cr (+35%), GNPA 3.5%/NNPA 2.1%; AL's carrying value ~₹64/share. “So we would take those actions to unlock this value at the right time.”
- *[May 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=d25ed8e8-c096-4919-b14b-1b1a488ac72f.pdf)* — Dheeraj Hinduja ties the unlocking explicitly to the listing route in his closing remarks, noting HHF is now the fourth-largest affordable housing finance company yet invisible in AL's share price. “Although HLF and HHF do not really figure as we see it showing a true value in Ashok Leyland shares today, but it will through the listing process unlock this.”
- *[Aug 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=689f94d3-7f58-4d2f-ac2f-3ad8541598de.pdf)* — RBI's final clearance to initiate the merger with NXT Digital is announced as the gate that opens the listing; Balaji then enumerates the full approval chain (valuers, swap ratio, RBI, exchanges, ROC, SEBI, NCLT, EGM) and guides to a minimum of two to three quarters. HLF AUM ₹50,430cr, HHF ₹14,265cr (both +25%), PAT ₹160cr, NNPA 1.63%, CAR 18.2%, AL stake 61.12%. “Very recently, HLF also received the final clearance from RBI to initiate a merger process with NXT Digital paving the way for its listing.”
- *[Nov 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=19a3f6bd-e48c-4a48-9fbb-e727c5bbf7a8.pdf)* — Balaji gives the capital-constraint reason for separating the finance arm: HLFL's growth is limited by cash and Tier-1 capital, with RBI pressing Ashok Leyland for further investment — the dependence a separate listing is meant to end. HLF AUM ₹52,635cr (+26%), HHF ₹14,903cr (+20%), PAT ₹196cr, book value ₹7,418cr, NNPA 1.59%. “So there is plenty of business opportunity and their business opportunities are restricted with the availability of the cash, availability of the money and the Tier-1 capital is also pretty low where RBI has been insisting on the requirement of more investment in Hinduja Leyland Finance.”
- *[Feb 2026](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=410a36e5-83ff-4aec-9393-43663d6e0bd8.pdf)* — After boards approved the Scheme on 25 Nov 2025, management concedes slippage but says all approvals are now in hand and the process is in final closure; Balaji again cites sub-peer Tier-1 as the reason AL keeps having to inject capital into HLF and HHF. Finance subsidiaries' quarterly PAT ₹220cr; HLF AUM ₹56,470cr (+18%), HHF ₹15,454cr (+16%). “Reverse merger of HLF with NDL Ventures had some initial delays, but now with all the necessary approvals in place, the process is being followed for a final closure.”
- *[Jun 2026](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=f872356b-64f1-4724-abe2-b196bd2b41b2.pdf)* — Completion guided to within one or two quarters, with the finance arm now the largest piece of the non-CV value: HLF AUM ~₹59,000cr (+24%) and PAT ₹491cr (+20%), HHF AUM ~₹16,000cr (+15%) and PAT ₹387cr (+4%), consolidated net NPA ~1.4%; Balaji still flags Tier-1 below peers as a reason AL may have to invest again. “Reverse merger of HLF with NBL Ventures is progressing as per plan and should get consummated within this or the next quarter.”
- *Scheme* — The NCLT-sanctioned rationale states HLFL needs growth capital and that becoming the listed entity widens access to public and investor capital — the capital-access argument management made on the calls, now formalised. “The Transferor company being a successful NBFC, will need growth capital to accelerate growth and believes that merging with the Transferor company will increase the avenues for raising growth capital both from public and interested investors thereby resulting in value enhancement for its shareholders.”
- *Scheme* — Beyond capital, the Scheme claims efficiency and governance gains for the separated entity: no duplicated administration, fewer overlapping compliances, higher net worth, focused management and listed-company governance standards. “(b) Greater efficiency in capital raising by the merged entity, and unfettered access to both cash flow generated by the business and external capital raising which can be deployed more efficiently to fund growth opportunities;”
- *Scheme* — Mechanics and cost of the separation: swap of 25 NDL shares of ₹10 for every 10 HLFL shares of ₹10, HLFL dissolved without winding up, Ashok Leyland diluted from 61.12% in HLFL to 59.64% in NDL, which becomes AL's material listed subsidiary; sanctioned by NCLT Mumbai on 3 November 2026 with appointed date 1 April 2026. “Consequently, Ashok Leyland's shareholding shall stand diluted from 61.12% in HLFL to 59.64% in NDL and NDL shall become the material listed subsidiary of the Company.”

*Not explained on the calls:* No standalone valuation, discount quantified, target raise, ROE goal, or why a reverse merger into a shell beat an IPO; dilution to 59.64% and its cost never discussed on any call.

### The business being separated — its own numbers

**Financial service (Financial Services segment — Hinduja Leyland Finance Limited / Hinduja Housing Finance, reported as the Group's financing component)** · unit ₹ crore · Revenue = Segment Revenue (gross, before deduction of inter-segmental revenue, which is reported only as a single unallocated line: ₹2.67 cr FY24, ₹1.12 cr FY25, ₹0.97 cr FY26). Operating profit = 'Segment Results — Financial service (after deducting interest expense on loan financing)', i.e. segment profit before interest and tax (EBIT-type), not EBITDA and not PBT. Segment PAT is not disclosed — tax is shown only at Group level. Note FY2024 is restated in the FY2025 report: revenue ₹4,749.66 cr and segment result ₹758.20 cr (AR2025 p.299) versus ₹4,836.96 cr and ₹845.50 cr as originally reported (AR2024 p.295); the figures below use the originally reported FY2024 numbers.

## CYIENT — Cyient Ltd.

**PROBABLE** (a filing's text names a demerger; no scheme filing names it yet) · **PRE-SPIN — study the parent; the pieces do not trade yet** · score 5.7/10 · spin-off · 8 filing(s) from CALLS, NSE, NSE-deep · first 2026-03-03, latest 2026-03-31

> **Listing:** NOT YET — scheme at 'announced' stage; the resulting company will list only after NCLT sanction, effectiveness and a record date; no listing timeline stated

**What is being separated, as the documents put it:** Semiconductor business (fabless chip design, turnkey ASICs, power products); no demerger scheme appears in these documents. — class `value_unlocking`.

- *Insiders:* Cyient committed up to $100mn, about $30mn already invested; first external round dilutes only 10-12%, Cyient retains majority. Promoter and promoter group hold 24.70% of parent post-buyback and did not tender.
- *What it reveals:* Semiconductors priced at $500mn ($4,650cr) post-money by EAAA while management says the parent's market attributes 'marginal, if not negative' value; still loss-making (H1 FY27 segment EBIT -Rs584mn), breakeven FY28; group non-current borrowings jumped to Rs22,506mn.
- *Selling pressure:* unclear — No record date, entitlement ratio or listing stated; separation funded privately, so no index-exclusion or distributed-share overhang is on file.
- *Parent or spin:* parent · *option pricing date:* not stated
- *Read next:* Semiconductors segment EBIT and borrowings in the 22 Oct 2026 results, plus the omitted 3 March 2026 filing.
- *In their words:* “Our goal is to build Cyient Semiconductors as a stand-alone business with its own governance, its own accountability and its own long-term optionality that includes potentially a future spin-off path.”

### Why the demerger — three years of calls and the scheme

The business being separated is Cyient's global semiconductor arm, carved out effective 1 April 2025 into Cyient Semiconductors Private Limited (plus Singapore, US, UK, Germany, India and Cayman step-downs) with its own CEO (Suman Narayan), CFO (Ramya Mohan) and board, and reported from Q1 FY26 as a fourth segment alongside DET, DLM and Others, with DET restated to exclude it. Management's stated reason is twofold: the semiconductor model is capital-hungry in a way the engineering-services parent is not — Krishna Bodanapu drew an explicit parallel to Cyient DLM, saying 'the way semiconductor business works is more like a DLM kind of a structure where you do have a higher capital investment, you have design, which takes upfront capital' — and the losses from that investment were being punished inside the listed parent. The numbers they cited: semiconductor FY26 revenue of only $25.7M (Q4 $7.2M, +5% QoQ, fourth straight sequential rise) against a Q4 EBIT loss of $2.8M; group EBIT margin contracted 254bps YoY to 9.5% 'primarily reflecting strategic investments in the semiconductor business'; stated maximum organic investment of $15M, later a committed envelope of 'up to $100 million' of which ~$30M was deployed and ~$70M remained; breakeven slipping from FY27 to 'late FY27, early FY28' to FY28. The problem they said separation solves is valuation: Bodanapu argued the market ascribes 'marginal, if not negative' value to the unit because an EV/EBIT multiple on a loss-making business goes negative, that Cyient shareholders were 'getting penalized' for it, and that continuing to fund it from the parent without establishing its value was 'unfair to shareholders'; against that, turnkey ASIC companies 'have commanded valuation multiples nearly 3x those of semiconductor services firms', rising further with owned IP. The chosen mechanism was an independent capital structure rather than a demerger: Kinetic Technologies ($85M, 82.9% stake, ~250 products, 100+ patents, doubling addressable market to ~$8.5bn) was funded by ~$80M of low-cost Singapore-entity debt on the semiconductor balance sheet, and in May 2026 the unit signed its first external round with EAAA Alternatives (ex-Edelweiss Alternatives) — INR 300 crore as INR 200 crore debt plus INR 100 crore equity at an INR 4,650 crore / $500M post-money equity valuation, roughly 6–7x revenue — closed in Q1 FY27 as $30M of fresh capital. CFO Ramya Mohan framed the structure as giving 'a dedicated capital base', 'real operational discipline and financial separation from the parent', and 'its own long-term optionality that includes potentially a future spin-off path', with debt deliberately preferred over a large equity issue 'to protect it against dilution'. Management was explicit that a comparable clean demerger of Cyient DLM is not contemplated, because of engineering/manufacturing interdependence, and that an own capital structure is itself the value-unlock avenue.

**How it evolved:** The idea surfaced as a structural carve-out announced complete on the 24 Jul 2025 Q1 FY26 call (new four-segment reporting, DET restated ex-semis, start-up framing), and on 16 Oct 2025 Bodanapu first attached a valuation thesis to it — 'create a DLM like story for Cyient's shareholders' plus the 3x ASIC-vs-services multiple argument — while capping organic investment at $15M and promising EBIT-neutrality in FY27. Through 18 Dec 2025 (Kinetic signing) and 22 Jan 2026 the rationale shifted from services to an IP/product company needing sustained R&D, and Kinetic was financed on the subsidiary's own Singapore-entity debt rather than parent cash. On 23 Apr 2026 the Board agreed in principle to explore an external debt-and-equity raise 'for the semiconductor business, which is a stand-alone business and the step-down subsidiary', with Bodanapu naming the real driver — the market ascribes marginal-to-negative value and Cyient shareholders are being penalised — and guiding to only 10–12% initial dilution; by 26 May 2026 the EAAA deal was signed at a $500M post-money valuation with a 'potentially a future spin-off path' named for the first time, and on 23 Jul 2026 the $30M round was reported closed while a clean DLM demerger was declined on the same call.

**What management expects from it:** For Cyient Semiconductors: dedicated long-cycle R&D capital, operational discipline and financial separation, ASSP gross margins of 50–60% versus services, EBIT breakeven in FY28, ASSP rising to 50–55% of mix, and an IP-led valuation (6–7x revenue, $500M) with optionality including a future spin-off. For Cyient: DET margins no longer dragged by semiconductor losses (group EBIT fell 254bps to 9.5%), no shareholder penalty, and value unlock via an independent, separately-funded structure.

**Point by point, with the source:**

- *CALL Jul 2025* — Carve-out of the semiconductor business into a separate wholly owned subsidiary with its own leadership and reporting segment is announced as complete, with DET restated to exclude it and the unit framed as a start-up investment. “Coming to the highlights for this quarter , It is my pleasure to announce that the Semiconductor business carve out process is completed as planned.”
- *CALL Jul 2025* — The unit is described as a separate subsidiary with its own leaders, management and structure, reported under a new four-segment structure (DET, DLM, Semiconductor, Others) precisely because its strategic plans differ. “The reason why we've split it out as such is it has very different strategic plans.”
- *CALL Oct 2025* — Bodanapu gives the first explicit value-unlock rationale: replicate for shareholders what the separately capitalised, listed Cyient DLM did, including the stated $15M cap on organic investment and FY27 EBIT-neutrality. “The opportunity here is to create a DLM like story for Cyient's shareholders through Cyient semiconductors.”
- *CALL Oct 2025* — The valuation arbitrage is quantified: turnkey ASIC and IP-owning businesses trade at multiples far above semiconductor services, which is why the unit must be valued on its own. “Historically, turnkey ASIC companies have commanded valuation multiples nearly 3x those of semiconductor services firms, and as we gain ownership and control over IP, these multiples increase even further.”
- *CALL Dec 2025* — The Kinetic Technologies majority stake (~250 ASSP products, 100+ patents, doubling addressable market to $8.5bn) is justified by the need for sustained R&D and owned IP — the capital-intensity argument for a separate balance sheet. “True product differentiation, scalable and profitable growth, and long -term shareholde r value in a semiconductor business is created through sustained investment in R&D, control of the semiconductor ecosystem for cost reduction, and the ownership of intellectual property and patents.”
- *CALL Apr 2026* — The Board agrees in principle to an external debt-and-equity fundraise, expressly ring-fenced to the stand-alone step-down subsidiary and driven by its growth and working-capital needs, alongside a INR 720 crore buyback at the parent. “I just want to repeat that this is for the semiconductor business, which is a stand -alone business and the step -down subsidiary of Cyient Limited.”
- *CALL Apr 2026* — Asked to reconcile a parent buyback with a subsidiary fundraise, Bodanapu states the core problem the separation solves: Cyient shareholders are being penalised for semiconductor losses, so an independent valuation and capital structure is needed. “So we want to make sure that the Cyient shareholders are not getting penalized for the performance of Cyient Semiconductor by establishing an independent valuation and an independent capital structure.”
- *CALL Apr 2026* — He quantifies the mispricing: on an EV/EBIT basis a loss-making unit carries marginal or negative value inside the listed parent, and funding it from Cyient without establishing value is unfair to shareholders (FY26 semi revenue $25.7M, Q4 EBIT -$2.8M). “Now in terms of what percentage of Cyient's market cap now that's for our invest ors to determine, which as I understand it, the value that's attributed to Cyient Semiconductor is marginal, if not negative, because if we just do a simple EBIT multiple, EV to EBIT multiple, then it actually becomes negative because it's a money -losing business.”
- *CALL Jun 2026* — On the 26 May 2026 semiconductor financing call, CFO Ramya Mohan answers 'why raise external debt when there is cash with the parent' by naming financial separation, governance and a possible future spin-off as the goal — the clearest statement of intent on the separation. “Our goal is to build Cyient Semiconduct ors as a stand -alone business with its own governance, its own accountability and its own long -term optionality that includes potentially a future spin -off path.”
- *CALL Jun 2026* — Bodanapu draws the explicit DLM parallel on capital intensity — upfront design capital — as the reason the unit needs its own capital structure and its own investor base, while keeping Cyient's up-to-$100M commitment ($30M already in, ~$70M available) intact. “So, we think it's better that Cyient Semiconductor has its own independent capital structure with the kind of investors that want to participate in that capital structure, and we thought this was a good starting point.”
- *CALL Jun 2026* — The round is announced as INR 300 crore (INR 200 crore debt plus INR 100 crore equity) at an INR 4,650 crore / $500M post-money equity valuation from EAAA Alternatives, roughly 6–7x revenue, after inbound interest from global funds and strategics; debt was chosen over a large equity issue to limit dilution. “But we made a deliberate choice not to issue a large amount of equity at this stage to protect it against dilution and preserve the shareholder value we are working to create.”
- *CALL Jul 2026* — The round is confirmed closed at $30M of fresh debt-and-equity capital at the $500M post-money valuation, framed as balance-sheet strength to fund the high-power ASSP development that is depressing operating profitability (breakeven now FY28, with ~$3M/quarter Kinetic amortisation). “I am pleased to announce that we have closed this round $30 million of fresh capital raised through a combination of debt and equity is in place.”

*Not explained on the calls:* No scheme of arrangement, demerger mechanics, record date, share-entitlement ratio, listing route or timetable for the stated spin-off path; no stranded-cost, tax or regulatory detail.

- *In their words:* “This created a pure play energy technology company in India that operates across the entire energy value chain, offering customers greater focus and agility, while unlocking shareholder value.”

### Why the demerger — three years of calls and the scheme

The separation at issue is the demerger of Siemens Limited's Energy Business into Siemens Energy India Limited (SEIL), under a Scheme approved by both boards on 14 May 2024, sanctioned by NCLT Mumbai on 25 March 2025 (effective 25 March 2025, appointed date 1 March 2025), with 356,120,505 shares issued 1:1 to Siemens Limited shareholders on 14 April 2025 and listing on BSE/NSE on 19 June 2025. The only explicit rationale management gives is in the Q4 FY25 press release: the demerger 'created a pure play energy technology company in India that operates across the entire energy value chain, offering customers greater focus and agility, while unlocking shareholder value' — i.e. focus/agility for customers plus value unlock for shareholders, mirroring the global carve-out of Siemens' energy business into Siemens Energy. Management frames the problem it solves as capturing a step-change in Indian energy demand that a conglomerate structure would serve less sharply: generation doubling from ~500 GW to ~1,000 GW, 500 GW renewables by 2030 ('two Germany's in the next seven to 10 years'), per-capita consumption of ~1,400 kWh versus one-third of the global average, NITI Aayog's $9–14 trillion to 2070, and CEA's upgraded 2030–36 plan adding 200+ GW of generation and ~800 GVA of transformation. The separated entity is a two-segment, eight-factory, ~4,500-person business — Power Transmission (transformers, GIS/switchgear, HVDC VSC, STATCOM/SynCon, services) and Power Generation (industrial and up-to-250 MW steam turbines, gas/steam service, ER&D 'local for global') — explicitly excluding coal plant additions, solar, wind and compressors. The post-separation entity has moved fast on capital: ₹7.4 billion of brownfield expansion (Kalwa transformers doubling 15,000→30,000 MVA; Sambhajinagar switchgear) and a ₹20.6 billion / ₹2,060 crore greenfield 30,000 MVA power transformer plant funded from internal accruals, rationale filed as 'very high and increasing demand for large power transformers', operating FY2030–32. Numbers cited around the separation: FY25 revenue ₹78 billion (+25%), orders +49% to ₹13,114 crore, backlog ₹162 billion (+47% to ₹16,205 crore), profit from operations 18.0% FY25 / 19.3% per the deck (18% ex 1.3% one-offs); H1 FY26 backlog ₹150→184 billion (+22.2%), revenue ₹34→43 billion (+27%), PFO 19.1%→20.7% (underlying 17.2%→18.9%), book-to-bill 1.5, exports +500 bps, and a maiden ₹4/share (200%) dividend. Separation costs and limits were disclosed rather than argued away: a ₹546 million stamp duty/transfer-fee provision, ~1.9% of H1 profit from 'accrual releases and stamp duty charges associated with demerger', the entity remaining legally separate from Siemens Energy AG with sales rights only for South Asia (India, Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Maldives) so that exports happen only when Siemens Energy requests them, and compressors (Siemens Energy Industrial Turbomachinery India, Baroda) plus wind (Siemens Gamesa, Chennai) still sitting in separate Indian companies outside SEIL. Crucially, in these texts nobody is named as having asked for the separation — no investor, lender, customer or partner demand is cited; it is presented as a promoter/parent-led structural decision, and the related question of Siemens Energy AG buying Siemens AG's stake was declined as 'between the two parents or the promoters'.

**How it evolved:** The idea pre-dates these transcripts: the filings record board approval of the Scheme on 14 May 2024, NCLT sanction on 25 March 2025, allotment on 14 April 2025 and listing on 19 June 2025, with the 24 November 2025 FY25 press release supplying the only stated rationale (pure play, focus and agility, unlocking shareholder value) and the Q4 margin drag from mix plus a ₹546 million stamp duty provision. At the first analyst and investor meet on 10 December 2025, management presented SEIL as 'an independent listed entity' and 'pure play energy leader', restated FY23–FY24 using Siemens Limited's Energy segment for comparability under Ind AS 103, and conceded the carve-out is partial — compressors and wind remain in separate Indian companies and any integration 'depend[s] very much on the headquarters strategy'. On 13 February 2026 the board turned the standalone balance sheet into capex, approving ₹2,060 crore for a new 30,000 MVA transformer factory from internal accruals. By the 15 May 2026 Q2/H1 FY26 call the framing had shifted from rationale to consequences: demerger stamp duty and accrual releases were still a ~1.9% one-off in H1 profit, management stressed SEIL and Siemens Energy 'are still today different companies' with South Asia-only sales rights, and the pending parent-to-parent stake transfer was left unanswered.

**What management expects from it:** A focused, agile pure-play covering the whole energy value chain, with shareholder value unlocked via the 1:1 listing. Standalone capital goes into transformer/switchgear capacity (₹7.4bn brownfield, ₹20.6bn greenfield, internal accruals). Margins to rise on operating leverage and export mix (H1FY26 20.7%; PG 17.7%→21.3%), funding a ₹4/share dividend. Siemens Limited's post-demerger prospects are never discussed.

**Point by point, with the source:**

- *Scheme* — The FY25 results press release gives the only explicit purpose statement for the separation: a pure-play energy technology company spanning the whole value chain, with customer focus/agility and shareholder value unlock. “This created a pure play energy technology company in India that operates across the entire energy value chain, offering customers greater focus and agility, while unlocking shareholder value.”
- *Scheme* — The legal mechanism and timeline: boards approved the Scheme on 14 May 2024 for the demerger of Siemens Limited's Energy Business under Sections 230–232, NCLT sanctioned it on 25 March 2025 with appointed date 1 March 2025. “The Scheme of Arrangement between the Company and Siemens Limited and their respective shareholders and creditors, was approved by the Board of Directors of the Company and Siemens Limited on 14 May 2024, at their respective meetings, providing for the demerger of Siemens Limited's Energy Business to the Company in compliance with Sections 230 to 232 and other applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 (the "Scheme").”
- *Scheme* — Consideration was a mirror 1:1 share entitlement to Siemens Limited shareholders on the 7 April 2025 record date — 356,120,505 shares allotted 14 April 2025, listed 19 June 2025 — i.e. a value-unlock demerger, not a cash sale. “in the ratio of 1 (One) fully paid-up equity share of the Company having face value of Rs. 2 (Rupees Two) each for every 1 (One) fully paid-up equity share of Rs. 2 (Rupees Two) each held in Siemens Limited”
- *Scheme* — The direct frictional cost of the separation disclosed in the accounts: a Rs. 546 million provision for stamp duty, transfer fees and registration charges on moving property titles from Siemens Limited. “During the year ended 30 September 2025, pursuant to the Scheme and applicable laws of India, stamp duty, transfer fees and other registration charges are payable by the Company on the transfer of the title of immovable properties / leasehold land from Siemens Limited to the Company. Accordingly, the Company had recorded a provision of Rs. 546 million towards these expenses.”
- *Scheme* — Four months post-listing the standalone board committed Rs. 2,060 crore of internal accruals to a ~30,000 MVA greenfield transformer plant (FY2030–32), justified purely by transformer demand — the clearest evidence of the focused entity deploying its own capital. “Domestic and global trend for energy transition and electrification has resulted in a very high and increasing demand for large power transformers.”
- *[Dec 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=7acc3738-badb-4ac1-aa4a-008b95d573c3.pdf)* — The December 10, 2025 meet was staged as the debut of a standalone company, positioning SEIL as a pure-play energy leader setting its own course after the demerger. “A company built on a legacy of innovation, now charting its own course as a pure play energy leader .”
- *[Dec 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=7acc3738-badb-4ac1-aa4a-008b95d573c3.pdf)* — Mendonca grounded the pure-play logic in whole-value-chain coverage against niche competitors — generation, transmission and industrial consumption in one entity. “So we are a company that only focus on the power sector and differently from other competitors
Siemens Energy goes through the entire value chain .”
- *[Dec 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=7acc3738-badb-4ac1-aa4a-008b95d573c3.pdf)* — Harish explained the comparability problem the separation created: FY23/FY24 had to be shown as Siemens Limited's Energy segment, with Ind AS 103 forcing an 8-month versus 12-month comparison from incorporation on 7 February 2024. “Because this is a first year and you would know for a new entity it's a bit different in terms of how do we compare numbers and to Consistency and comparability what we've done is we've also taken the Energy segment which was reported hitherto in Siemens limited as a segment in the past two years .”
- *[Dec 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=7acc3738-badb-4ac1-aa4a-008b95d573c3.pdf)* — The carve-out is deliberately incomplete: compressors sit in Siemens Energy Industrial Turbomachinery India (Baroda) and wind in Siemens Gamesa (Chennai), so SEIL is not the full parent portfolio in India. “The portfolio that we do in SEIL is everything but compressors and wind, but we are
serving the country as a whole.”
- *[Dec 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=7acc3738-badb-4ac1-aa4a-008b95d573c3.pdf)* — Asked whether the missing compressor business would be folded in to align SEIL with the parent portfolio, management said the decision is not theirs. “If you ask me about integr ation. This is something that I cannot answer you because we are depend very much on the headquarters strategy when they want to do that.”
- *[Dec 2025](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=7acc3738-badb-4ac1-aa4a-008b95d573c3.pdf)* — A structural limit of the separated entity: the export leg is controlled by the parent's global factory network, so SEIL can plan only the domestic market. “But when is about export actually the headquarters side. Because it's their responsibility to decide for a given country for a given customer what is the most suitable factory to supply”
- *[May 2026](https://www.bseindia.com/stockinfo/AnnPdfOpen.aspx?Pname=197a7a32-b6e5-4070-98a3-4e6d3b8f22ed.pdf)* — Mendonca spelled out the post-separation relationship: SEIL and Siemens Energy are still distinct companies, Siemens Energy is only a shareholder, and SEIL's own sales rights cover India plus Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Maldives. “We have to bear in mind that SEIL
and Siemens Energy, they are still today different companies, right? So, Siemens Energy is a shareholder in our
company and the SEIL has the sales rights and the responsibility to make business in the South Asia, as we call it.”

*Not explained on the calls:* No stated initiator, no synergy/dis-synergy or valuation quantification, no royalty/trademark economics, nothing on Siemens Limited's residual company, why now, or why compressors and wind were excluded.

### The business being separated — its own numbers

**Siemens Energy India Limited (SEIL) — Siemens Limited's demerged Energy Business, comprising the Power Transmission and Power Generation segments** · unit ₹ million · Operating profit = 'Profit from operations' (segment result / EBIT), i.e. revenue less cost of goods sold, depreciation & amortisation and other segment costs, before other income, finance costs, exceptional items and tax; it is the CODM's performance measure. ### Why the demerger — three years of calls and the scheme

The business being separated is the steel business undertaking of Bhushan Power & Steel Ltd. (BPSL) — the 4.5 MTPA integrated plant in Odisha that JSW acquired out of IBC on 26 March 2021 at 2.75 MTPA and expanded to 3.5 MTPA (Q4 FY23) and 4.5 MTPA (Q2 FY25). On 3 December 2025 the Board approved hiving it out by slump sale on a going-concern basis to JSW Sambalpur Steel Ltd (since renamed JSW JFE Steel Ltd) for cash consideration of Rs.24,483 crore, with JFE Steel Corporation, Japan — a strategic partner since 2009 — subscribing 50% of the holding company JSW Kalinga Steel Ltd for Rs.15,750 crore in two equal Rs.7,875 crore tranches, leaving the entity 50:50 and deconsolidated from JSW Steel at 31 March 2026. Management framed it as growth funding plus balance-sheet repair, not a disposal: the filing says the deal secures growth "in a financially prudent manner… across business cycles" towards 50 MTPA in India by FY31, and on the May 2026 call Jayant Acharya quantified ~Rs.37,000 crore of deleveraging (~Rs.30,000 crore done by March, a further ~Rs.7,900 crore from JFE's second tranche by end-June), leverage down to 1.81x, net debt Rs.54,000 crore, a credit-rating outlook uplift, and revised caps (gearing 1.75x→1.25x, leverage 3.75x→3.00x, comfort below 2.5x). The stated problems solved were capital constraint and single-engine growth — Acharya called it a "double engine of growth" enabling multiple simultaneous projects (62 MTPA standalone by FY32 plus 16 MTPA across the JFE and POSCO JVs, ~80 MTPA with Ohio) — plus access to JFE's "best-in-class technology" for high-end value-added grades. In parallel, the Piombino Steel Ltd. merger into JSW Steel was approved the same day to let JSW hold BPSL directly, "enhancing strategic focus without minority shareholders' involvement" (JSW Shipping & Logistics, a promoter entity, held 17.35%) and to give the parent "additional cash to pursue its growth aspirations." Q4 FY26 booked an Rs.18,051 crore exceptional gain on the slump sale, with tax largely absorbed by BPSL's carry-forward losses and unabsorbed depreciation.

**How it evolved:** The idea surfaced as a fully-formed board decision on 3 December 2025, when JSW simultaneously approved the JFE 50:50 JV/slump sale and the Piombino Steel merger, signing the JV agreement, business transfer agreement and share subscription agreement the same day; the Jan 2026, Oct 2025 and earlier call transcripts are image-only, so no pre-announcement management discussion is in this record. CCI cleared it on 20 January 2026, the slump sale completed 27 March 2026, and the May 14, 2026 call first quantified the outcome (Rs.37,000 crore deleveraging, 1.81x leverage, Rs.18,051 crore gain, deconsolidation) while widening the logic into a second JV with POSCO (agreement signed April 2026 for a 6 MTPA Odisha greenfield via Saffron Resources, ~Rs.508.8 crore subscription) and raising the capacity target from 50 MTPA by FY31 to 62 MTPA by FY32 plus 16 MTPA in JVs. The Piombino arm closed later: shareholders approved on 21 August 2026 (94.86% of votes, 97.20% of public votes), NCLT sanctioned on 16 October 2026 and the scheme became effective 31 October 2026 with appointed date 1 January 2026.

**What management expects from it:** For JSW Steel: ~Rs.37,000 crore deleveraging, 1.81x leverage, Rs.54,000 crore net debt, rating uplift, tighter covenant caps, and capacity for Rs.2.26 lakh crore of capex toward 62 MTPA by FY32. For the JV (JSW JFE Steel): accelerated expansion of the 4.5 MTPA BPSL asset using JFE's best-in-class technology into high-end value-added grades, plus secured iron ore and coal supply from the parent.

- *[May 2026](https://jsw-steel-s3.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/jsw-steel-images/uploads/2026/05/JSWSteel-Earnings-May14-2026_vF.pdf)* — Ashwin Bajaj clarified the reporting consequence: BPSL leaves consolidated EBITDA from March-end and appears only via equity accounting, and FY27 guidance of 29.75 mt production / 28.6 mt sales excludes JV volumes. “BPSL has been deconsolidated at March-end. And the numbers for BPSL will not be part of financials of EBITDA.”
- *Scheme* — The 3 December 2025 filing set out the mechanics: a slump sale of the BPSL steel undertaking into JSW Sambalpur for Rs.24,483 crore cash, with JSW Kalinga ending up 50:50 between JSW Steel and JFE. “Transfer of BPSL Steel business undertaking, by way of slump sale on a going concern basis to JSW Sambalpur Steel Limited ("JSW Sambalpur") for a cash consideration of Rs 24,483 crores, subject to customary closing adjustments as agreed in the transaction documents.”
- *Scheme* — JFE's cheque was Rs.15,750 crore for 50% of JSW Kalinga, paid in two equal tranches, with equal board rights (two directors in JSW Kalinga, three in JSW Sambalpur) and customary affirmative consents. “JFE will invest/ acquire 50% equity stake in JSW Kalinga at an aggregate consideration of Rs. 15,750 crores in two equal tranches, as per the terms of definitive documents entered into for this purpose.”

*Not explained on the calls:* No valuation basis for Rs.24,483 crore or JFE's Rs.15,750 crore, no investor/lender request cited, no JV capex or return targets, and pre-announcement calls are unreadable scans.

## AIIL — Authum Investment & Infrastructure Ltd.

**PROBABLE** (a filing's text names a demerger; no scheme filing names it yet) · **PRE-SPIN — study the parent; the pieces do not trade yet** · score 5.0/10 · spin-off · 4 filing(s) from NSE · first 2025-11-12, latest 2026-10-10

> **Listing:** NOT YET — scheme at 'nclt_sanction' stage; the resulting company will list only after NCLT sanction, effectiveness and a record date; no listing timeline stated

**The stages, as filed:** meetings (2025-11-12) → nclt_sanction (2026-07-12)

**What is being separated, as the documents put it:** not stated — no demerger of any Authum business is disclosed in these filings — class `not stated`.

- *Insiders:* ESOP 2025 excludes promoters/promoter group and >10% directors; Mentor Capital Limited, Promoter, subscribes up to Rs. 2,450 crore NCRPS. New-entity insider stakes not stated.
- *What it reveals:* No separation disclosed. Filings instead show Rs. 8880.02 crore free reserves/premium as on September 30, 2025, a 4:1 bonus, 88.37% of ISARC (net worth Rs. 353.29 crore), and 25% of Vibhav Energy.
- *Selling pressure:* unclear — No demerged entity, share allotment or index event is described in the documents.
- *Parent or spin:* neither · *option pricing date:* not stated
- *Read next:* NCLT order dated July 27, 2026 refusing the scheme of arrangement in the Wind World (India) resolution plan
- *In their words:* “However, since the scheme of arrangement forming part of the Resolution Plan, was not approved by the NCLT vide the NCLT Approval Order, the Consortium revised the transaction structure / structure for implementation of the Resolution Plan (pursuant to such flexibility under the Resolution Plan), which was approved by the implementation and monitoring committee vide its resolution dated August 31, 2026 (“Revised Structure”).”

### Why the demerger — three years of calls and the scheme

These texts do not contain any explanation by AIIL management of a separation, demerger or spin-off of one of AIIL's own businesses — there are no earnings-call transcripts on file ('no transcripts on file') and none of the nine filings is a scheme of arrangement for AIIL, so no management rationale, no investor/lender/partner demand and no financial targets for such a separation can be reconstructed from them. The only business separation described anywhere in the material is the splitting of a third party, Wind World (India) Limited (WWIL), between the two members of the consortium that acquired it under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016: the filing of July 28, 2026 states that Inox Neo Energies Limited (INEL, the Lead Member) and/or its affiliates would take (i) the IPP and power sale undertaking and (ii) the operations and maintenance (O&M) business of WWIL, while AIIL and/or its affiliates would take 'certain identified real estate / assets'. AIIL's financial commitment for that identified-asset leg was approximately INR 350 crore, which the October 10, 2026 filing confirms was fully remitted to WWIL (net of TDS filed on WWIL's behalf). That filing also records that the scheme of arrangement forming part of the Resolution Plan was NOT approved by the NCLT in its order of July 27, 2026, so the Consortium used the flexibility in the Resolution Plan to adopt a 'Revised Structure' cleared by the implementation and monitoring committee on August 31, 2026; the debt/equity infusion option that was to go into WWIL was redirected to Vibhav Energy Private Limited (VEPL), an implementation entity of the Lead Member and a subsidiary of Inox Green Energy Services Limited, via a INR 100 crore inter-corporate deposit dated September 28, 2026 that converted on October 9, 2026 into 10,00,00,000 shares, or 25% of VEPL on a fully diluted basis. The stated reason AIIL gives for that 25% stake is only that 'the target entity has strong potential for value creation, and it also aligns with our objective of portfolio diversification' — VEPL had nil turnover in FY2023-24, FY2024-25 and FY2025-26 and negative net worth of INR (0.1) crore at March 31, 2026. The remaining filings concern unrelated capital actions rather than any separation: a 4:1 bonus issue (67,93,80,400 shares, out of Rs. 8,880.02 crore of free reserves/premium at September 30, 2025) approved by the board on November 28, 2025 and by shareholders on December 31, 2025; a Rs. 2,450 crore 0.01% NCRPS private placement to promoter Mentor Capital Limited redeemable at a 6.5% IRR over 15 years, approved November 17, 2025; an ESOP Scheme 2025 of 5,00,000 options including for subsidiary employees; a further Rs. 101.625 crore rights-issue subscription in 88.37%-owned ISARC 'to meet its capital requirement for general business operations'; and the NCLT's July 7, 2026 rejection of AIIL's resolution plan for Vas Infrastructure Limited, with the company stating 'there is no impact on the business operations of the Company'. In short, on these documents alone the question's premise — that AIIL is separating one of its businesses — is not evidenced, and the only documented separation is of WWIL's businesses between AIIL and INEL, driven by the structure of a court-supervised insolvency acquisition rather than by any explained strategic or stakeholder pressure.

**How it evolved:** With no transcripts on file, the only traceable sequence is in the filings: the WWIL resolution plan dated February 13, 2026 (addendum May 20, 2026), intimated February 20, 2026, already envisaged splitting WWIL's IPP/power-sale undertaking and O&M business to INEL and identified real estate/assets to AIIL. The July 28, 2026 filing reported NCLT approval of that plan on July 27, 2026 and restated the INR 350 crore commitment. The October 10, 2026 filing then disclosed that the NCLT did not approve the scheme of arrangement inside the plan, forcing a Revised Structure approved on August 31, 2026, under which AIIL's optional infusion went into INEL's implementation entity VEPL as a INR 100 crore ICD converted to a 25% equity stake on October 9, 2026. Separately, on July 11, 2026 AIIL disclosed the NCLT's July 7, 2026 rejection of its Vas Infrastructure resolution plan, with no impact on operations.

**What management expects from it:** Nothing is stated for AIIL itself. For the WWIL split, the documents only allocate assets — INEL's affiliates take the IPP/power-sale and O&M businesses; AIIL takes identified real estate/assets for ~INR 350 crore plus 25% of VEPL for INR 100 crore, justified solely as 'strong potential for value creation' and 'portfolio diversification'. No margin, capital-release, valuation or focus expectation is quantified anywhere.

**Point by point, with the source:**

- *Scheme* — The separation in these documents is the carve-up of WWIL between the two consortium members: INEL takes the IPP/power-sale undertaking and the O&M business, AIIL takes identified real estate/assets. “The Resolution Plan submitted by the consortium of INEL and the Company inter alia envisaged that INEL as the Lead Member and/or its affiliates shall acquire (i) the IPP and power sale undertaking ; and (ii) the operations and maintenance (O&M ) business of WWIL, while the Company and/or its affiliates shall acquire certain identified real estate / assets from WWIL.”
- *Scheme* — AIIL's leg of the split was sized at approximately INR 350 crore, and the October 10, 2026 filing confirms the full amount was remitted to WWIL net of TDS. “The financial commitment of the Company under the Resolution Plan as consideration for the purchase of certain identified assets of WWIL was INR 350,00,00,000 (Indian Rupees Three Hundred and Fifty Crore).”
- *Scheme* — The scheme of arrangement embedded in the Resolution Plan was rejected by the NCLT in its July 27, 2026 approval order, so the consortium re-engineered the implementation structure, cleared by the implementation and monitoring committee on August 31, 2026. “However, since the scheme of arrangement forming part of the Resolution Plan, was not approved by the NCLT vide the NCLT Approval Order, the Consortium revised the transaction structure / structure for implementation of the Resolution Plan (pursuant to such flexibility under the Resolution Plan), which was approved by the implementation and monitoring committee vide its resolution dated August 31, 2026 (“ Revised Structure ”).”
- *Scheme* — Under the Revised Structure, AIIL's infusion option moved from WWIL to VEPL, an INEL implementation entity: a INR 100 crore ICD dated September 28, 2026 converted on October 9, 2026 into 10 crore shares, 25% of VEPL fully diluted. “In terms of the Revised Structure, the Lead Member and the Company had an option to agree on terms and conditions for infusion by the Company of debt / equity in Vibhav Energy Private Limited, one of implementation entities of the Lead Member (“ VEPL”).”
- *Scheme* — The only stated rationale for AIIL's 25% VEPL stake is value-creation potential and portfolio diversification, despite VEPL reporting nil turnover in each of FY2023-24, FY2024-25 and FY2025-26 and net worth of INR (0.1) crore at March 31, 2026. “We believe the target entity has strong potential for value creation, and it also aligns with our objective of portfolio diversification.”
- *Scheme* — A separate insolvency acquisition did not survive: the NCLT rejected AIIL's resolution plan for Vas Infrastructure Limited on July 7, 2026, and AIIL said this changed nothing operationally. “We would further like to state that on account of the aforesaid rejection of the resolution plan there is no impact on the business operations of the Company.”
- *Scheme* — Capital actions in the window are expansionary and promoter/subsidiary-funding oriented, not separation-related: a 4:1 bonus issue of 67,93,80,400 shares out of Rs. 8,880.02 crore of reserves at September 30, 2025, taking paid-up equity from 16,98,45,100 to 84,92,25,500 shares. “The Board has recommended issuance of Bonus Shares by way of capitalization of reserves, in ratio of 4:1 i.e. 4 (four) new fully paid-up Equity Shares of Re. 1/- each (Rupee One only) for every 1(one) existing fully paid-up Equity Shares of Re. 1/- each (Rupees One only) held by the eligible shareholders as on the Record Date, subject to shareholders approval through postal ballot and any other applicable regulatory and statutory approvals consents, permissions, conditions and sanctions as may be required.”
- *Scheme* — Shareholders approved a Rs. 2,450 crore NCRPS private placement to promoter Mentor Capital Limited on November 17, 2025, priced at Rs. 1,000 per Rs. 10 face-value share, 0.01% non-cumulative dividend, 15-year tenure, redeemed at premium for a 6.5% IRR. “NCRPS shall be redeemed at premium at the end of the tenure to provide IRR of 6.5% on the issue price.”
- *Scheme* — AIIL kept funding its 88.37%-held ARC subsidiary ISARC rather than separating it, subscribing 40,65,00,000 rights shares with Rs. 101.625 crore paid as 25% application money on August 18, 2026. “Currently, Authum Investment & Infrastructure Limited is holding 88.37% share capital of ISARC and on account of Rights Issues offered by ISARC, the Company has accepted to invest further serving the subsidiary to meet its capital requirement for general business operations.”
- *Scheme* — The ESOP Scheme 2025 (up to 5,00,000 options, max 3,00,000 per employee, extended to subsidiary employees) explicitly contemplates adjustment on a merger/demerger but states no demerger plan for AIIL. “RESOLVED FURTHER THAT , in case of any corporate action(s) such as rights issues, bonus issues, split/consolidation of shares, change in capital structure, merger/demerger, the outstanding ESOPs, granted/to be granted, under the Scheme 2025 shall be suitably adjusted for such number of ESOPs/equity shares, and/or the exercise price, as may be required.”

*Not explained on the calls:* No transcripts or scheme document supplied; nothing explains any AIIL demerger, why NCLT rejected the scheme, the revised structure's economics, VEPL's nil-revenue valuation, or who requested separation.

- *Insiders:* "No promoter, director, key managerial personnel or related party of the Company will receive any special rights, differential consideration or economic benefit"; buyers not promoter group; 3.8 million ESOP shares to be awarded
- *What it reveals:* Sale prices above peer medians (7.5x and 12.5x); Rs. 2,256 crore (~USD 237 million) programme versus Rs. 1,159 crore FY26 revenue, with ~Rs. 1,255 crore expected disposal gain; retained defence/XiDA show 20%+ EBITDA and Rs. 4,557 crore Assured Forecast Visibility
- *Selling pressure:* unlikely — Cash slump sale, no shares distributed: "There will be no change in the shareholding pattern of the Company"
- *Parent or spin:* parent · *option pricing date:* not stated
- *Read next:* Q2 FY27 results: whether Phase 2 (USD 152.35/206.30 million) closed and the ~Rs. 1,255 crore disposal gain and proceeds deployment
- *In their words:* “The proposed slump sale is consistent with the Company's stated strategic objective of divesting its aerospace engineering services business and realigning and re-deploying its capital resources towards identified growth priorities.”

### Why the demerger — three years of calls and the scheme

Management framed the separation as removing structurally loss-making, margin-dilutive engineering services so capital and bandwidth can be redeployed into manufacturing-led aerospace, defence, space and ESAI under the Power 930 goal of Rs 9,000 crore revenue by FY2030. Phase 1 was the Heavy Engineering, Automotive and Energy engineering services practice — Rs 282 crore of FY25 revenue that de-grew 3% (automotive plus heavy engineering de-grew 7% to Rs 238 crore), 24% of turnover, and whose negative margins dragged a 19.1% core EBITDA down to 13.8% at enterprise level (19% vs 14% in Q1 FY26; 21.4% vs 16.2% in 9M FY26); it was sold to Akkodis on 26 May 2026 for USD 30.63 million (USD 17.42m at close, USD 5.81m deferred 12 months, USD 7.4m earnout on EBITDA to 30 June 2027), booking Rs 17.78 crore of FY26 exceptional cost (Rs 9.8 crore transaction cost plus Rs 7.98 crore fair-value hit on Epcogen, sold below book) against an expected Rs 175 crore gain, or Rs 41 per share. Phase 2 went further and sold the profitable Aerospace engineering services business — 31% of FY25 consolidated turnover (Rs 3,225.88 million) and 11.3% of net worth — carved into a New India Co and a Swiss Overseas HoldCo with step-downs in Germany, France, UK, Canada and the US, for USD 152.35 million of business-transfer consideration and up to USD 206.30 million of share consideration (Tranche 1 USD 77.70m for 51%; Tranche 2 USD 76.02m plus up to USD 52.58m performance-linked for the residual 49% after 24 months), the whole programme being a minimum Rs 1,685 crore and about Rs 2,256 crore (USD 237 million) with an expected disposal gain of roughly Rs 1,255 crore. The stated problems solved were four: margin dilution from non-core verticals hit by the German/European automotive downturn (add solution GmbH, Volkswagen-dependent, later put into voluntary solvent liquidation in October 2026 after continuous losses, and the cause of an unrecognised deferred tax asset that pushed the FY26 tax rate to 36%); Epcogen's energy business never reaching critical mass; management bandwidth consumed by resetting non-core while the core needed execution; and above all funding — DAC at about Rs 1,200 crore, MAC at Rs 300 crore, DAL at Rs 120 crore (Rs 1,550-1,600 crore of facilities) plus roughly Rs 600 crore of two ESAI and two aerospace acquisitions, Rs 2,100-2,250 crore in total, which management insisted would be met without equity dilution and without incremental long-term debt. For aerospace specifically the logic was different from the non-core logic: the unit would grow faster inside a larger platform than alone, the 51/49 structure lets AXISCADES capture two years of that accelerated growth and sell the rest at FY28 scale, and exiting services lets AXISCADES move up the value chain from design (the architect's 3%) to manufacturing (the builder's 97%). No lender or named investor was said to have demanded the separation; the push came from the Chairman after he resumed in late FY25, a strategic advisor engaged by Q1 FY26, Zinnov consulting on automotive, and repeated analyst questioning — with strategic investment from OEMs into AAIPL having stayed 'in the works' as the alternative funding route that did not land.

**How it evolved:** It surfaced on the Jun 2025 (Q4 FY25) call only as 'evaluating and recalibrating' non-core heavy engineering, energy and automotive called growth- and margin-dilutive, with Zinnov engaged on automotive; by Aug 2025 (Q1 FY26) a strategic advisor was formally engaged on 'optimizations and restructuring'. On the Nov 2025 (Q2 FY26) call it became an explicit divestment of 'non-yielding, non-profitable assets' sized to fund DAC/DAL/MAC without debt or dilution, targeted for completion by March 2026 and called the Chairman's personal goal; on the Feb 2026 (Q3 FY26) call it was 'very much on track', with the 30% of headcount sitting in non-core identified as part of it. By the Jun 2026 (Q4 FY26) calls Phase 1 had been signed on 26 May 2026 to Akkodis for USD 30.63 million while Phase 2 — much larger — had 'delayed a bit' and was pushed to H1 FY27; the filings then show Phase 2 (Aerospace, USD 152.35m plus up to USD 206.30m) approved 12 June 2026, shareholders approving 27 July 2026, Phase 1 closing 1 October 2026 with USD 4.1 million held back, and add solution GmbH dissolved on 25 September 2026.

**What management expects from it:** Retained aerospace, defence and ESAI already earn 20%+ EBITDA versus 15.3% enterprise, improving 150-200bps yearly; Rs 2,256 crore of proceeds and a ~Rs 1,255 crore gain self-fund Rs 2,100-2,250 crore of capex plus four acquisitions without equity dilution; headcount falls 2,800 to 1,200 and revenue per employee rises Rs 42 lakh to Rs 1.2 crore; aerospace services grows faster inside Akkodis.
